en: The Sun heats ocean water, turning it into invisible water vapor that rises into the cooler atmosphere.
Flowing water in rivers physically breaks large rocks into smaller pebbles by constantly tumbling them against each other.
Lichens secrete acids that slowly dissolve solid basalt rock surfaces to create the first thin layers of soil.
The Sun's immense gravitational pull keeps the eight planets moving in elliptical orbits instead of flying into space.
A collapsing cloud of gas and dust in a nebula heats up until nuclear fusion ignites a new star.
The Moon orbits Earth, changing the angle of sunlight hitting its surface and creating its different visible phases.
The Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, causing warm air to rise and cooler air to rush in, creating wind.
Magma rises through vents in Mayon Volcano because it is less dense than the surrounding solid rock.
Warm surface water from the equator flows toward the poles, transferring heat and warming colder coastal climates.
Intense underground heat and pressure squeeze limestone, transforming it into a new metamorphic rock called marble.
The Moon passes directly between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on Earth and causing a solar eclipse.
Tectonic plates sliding past each other build up stress until the rock suddenly fractures, releasing energy as earthquake waves.
